title: Reward Hacking Challenges Oversight of Autonomous Research Agents

paper.title: Reward Hacking Challenges Oversight of Autonomous Research Agents
paper.abstract:
Abstract Autonomous research agents can design experiments, evaluate results, and write reports,
giving them control over both a scientific result and the evidence used to support it.
This creates a risk of reward hacking: meeting the reward criteria without achieving the intended goal. We study (1) how often models reward-hack without instructions
to do so, (2) how effective and detectable their methods are when hacking is allowed, and
(3) how they adapt when an LLM review panel returns its decision and reasons. Across 17 language
models and 38 tasks, the spontaneous reward-hacking rate is 30.5 % 30.5\% on open-ended
research-pipeline tasks and 2.9 % 2.9\% on task-specific kernels. When hacking is allowed on
tasks whose pass thresholds exceed our best compliant baselines, 505 / 677 505/677 attempts
( 74.6 % 74.6\% ) are confirmed reward hacks: they both clear the threshold and receive
mechanism-verification panel confirmation of an evaluation exploit. An LLM panel reviewing
only submitted code and reported scores misses 33 / 505 33/505 confirmed hacks ( 6.5 % 6.5\% ).
Direct methods that achieve the highest scores are often easy to
detect, while less direct methods evade more often. In a five-round loop, the number of
model-task pairs with an evasion rises from 7 to 56. Among 79 pairs evaluated under two feedback conditions, cumulative evasion reaches 40.5 % 40.5\% with detailed feedback and 20.3 % 20.3\% with generic rejection. The detailed condition includes the review decision, reasons, and attempt history, so this comparison does not isolate the effect of explanations.
These findings highlight the need for stronger defenses, including metrics kept outside the agent’s control and independent recomputation on data chosen to expose likely exploits.

The detailed condition includes the review decision, reasons, and attempt history, so this comparison does not isolate the effect of explanations. These findings highlight the need for stronger defenses, including metrics kept outside the agent’s control and independent recomputation on data chosen to expose likely exploits. 1 Introduction Figure 1: From spontaneous reward hacking to adaptive evasion under oversight. Research agents produce both results and the evidence used to assess them, motivating three progressively deeper tests of this workflow. Top, the shared research process; the dashed feedback loop applies only to E3. Bottom, E1: Spontaneous reward hacking. We measure hacking under ordinary task instructions, without a request to hack. E2: Hacking effectiveness and detectability. We evaluate exploits when hacking is permitted; the bars illustrate exploits exceeding thresholds that compliant baselines do not meet. The quality review rates the hacking method on efficacy, generality, craft, and novelty, each on a 1–10 scale. E3: Adaptation to oversight. Given an explicit evasion objective and review feedback, agents revise their methods, and some exploits remain undetected. The terracotta trace passes through the reviewer to illustrate a missed exploit. Arrows between E1–E3 indicate the progression of research questions. The illustrations are schematic. Research agents can propose methods, write code, run experiments and draft papers with little supervision ( Lu et al., 2024 ; Yamada et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . These capabilities may accelerate scientific work, but they also change how its reliability is established. An agent that controls data processing, evaluation and reporting can influence both a result and the evidence used to judge it. Delegating these stages together can weaken the separation between producing a scientific claim and independently verifying it (Fig. 1 ). Reward hacking makes this problem concrete. An agent may obtain credit on an evaluation metric without demonstrating the capability that the metric is intended to measure ( Amodei et al., 2016 ; Krakovna et al., 2020 ; Skalse et al., 2022 ) . It may read evaluation labels, train on the test set or change the grader. In research workflows, the result can include plausible code, favorable scores and an apparently coherent account of the experiment. The concern is therefore not only an incorrect conclusion, but evidence that makes an unsupported conclusion appear justified. We study reward hacking at inference time, when an agent exploits a task metric or grader, rather than optimization of a reward model during training ( Khalaf et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) . We use evaluation exploit for a method that takes advantage of evaluation inputs, rules or reporting to obtain credit without satisfying the task’s intended evaluation protocol. This includes gaming a misspecified metric without changing its code. An unconventional method that preserves the protocol and demonstrates the required capability is not an exploit. The risk resembles p-hacking, in which researchers try multiple analyses and selectively report favorable results ( Simmons et al., 2011 ) . A research agent can make such choices across the workflow, leaving the decisive deviation in a data dependency, an evaluation rule or an unstated assumption rather than an obvious error in the report. Prior studies formalize proxy gaming and over-optimization ( Skalse et al., 2022 ; Pan et al., 2022 ; Gao et al., 2022 ) , document strategic behavior under oversight ( Greenblatt et al., 2024 ; Meinke et al., 2024 ) , and evaluate coding agents that exploit visible tests or hard-code outputs ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Lodkaew et al., 2026 ; Zhong et al., 2025 ) . Other work shows that optimization against monitors can encourage obfuscation ( Baker et al., 2025 ; Terekhov et al., 2025 ; Najt et al., 2026 ) . These findings motivate examining how control over research design, evaluation and reporting affects the detectability of an exploit, and whether review remains effective when an agent is explicitly directed to revise its strategy to evade detection. We examine these questions across 17 language models and 38 tasks in three settings (E1, E2, and E3). E1 measures the occurrence of reward hacking under ordinary task instructions, without asking agents to hack. E2 tests the effectiveness and detectability of evaluation exploits when hacking is explicitly permitted on tasks whose thresholds exceed compliant baselines. We compare artifact review with additional trajectory inspection and independent recomputation. E3 tests adversarial adaptation: agents are explicitly tasked with revising caught attempts to evade review, with up to five attempts under either detailed feedback or a generic rejection. The results distinguish the occurrence of an exploit from its detectability. Reward hacking is about ten times more frequent on open-ended research-pipeline tasks than on task-specific kernels. Direct leakage is common but usually visible, whereas some methods resembling ordinary research choices pass artifact review and remain unresolved after full-trajectory inspection. In the adversarial setting, cumulative evasion is higher with detailed feedback than with retry-only review over the same number of allowed rounds. Together, these results identify both existing review blind spots and the potential for an agent pursuing an evasion objective to exploit them through repeated interaction. Figure 2: Evaluation settings. (a) Setting 1 measures spontaneous reward hacking in one complete agent session per model–task pair, without instructions to hack. A full-trajectory evaluator uses the trajectory, submission, and instrumented checks. (b) Setting 2 allows reward hacking on baseline-exceeding tasks. An LLM review panel that sees the submitted code and reported score, but not the trajectory or mechanism summary, tests whether it detects the method (Metric 1), conditional on threshold passage and mechanism verification; a separate panel rates quality (Metric 2). (c) Setting 3 returns the review panel’s decision, reasons, and the attempt history to the agent for up to five rounds. We distinguish evaluation exploits from legitimate success using independent execution evidence and a verification panel’s comparison of the artifact with the model’s mechanism summary ( § 3.1 ). Our findings show why passing an automated review is not equivalent to establishing the validity of a research claim. Expanding the use of research agents therefore requires verification procedures that can test their claims using criteria and evidence outside the agents’ control. 2 Related work Reward hacking in LLM agents Reward hacking, or specification gaming, is the optimization of a proxy at the expense of the intended objective ( Amodei et al., 2016 ; Krakovna et al., 2020 ) . Prior work formalizes when proxies are hackable ( Skalse et al., 2022 ) and how misspecification and over-optimization scale ( Pan et al., 2022 ; Gao et al., 2022 ) . Large models have tampered with their reward ( Denison et al., 2024 ) , behaved strategically under perceived oversight ( Greenblatt et al., 2024 ) , pursued in-context schemes ( Meinke et al., 2024 ) , and hacked tasks at inference time ( Khalaf et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ) . These behaviors have also motivated evaluations-based safety cases ( Balesni et al., 2024 ) . The closest benchmarks study coding agents that game visible tests or hard-code outputs ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Lodkaew et al., 2026 ) . Zhong et al. (2025) , for example, make unit tests conflict with the specification, so every pass is an exploit. We instead set pass thresholds above measured compliant baselines and use research tasks whose graders are loose proxies rather than unit tests. Monitoring is a common response ( Zheng et al., 2023 ; Korbak et al., 2025 ) . Guardian models may screen actions before execution ( Huang et al., 2026a ) or return a risk label with a rationale ( Huang et al., 2026b ) . Their reliability is imperfect: Yang et al. (2026) find a persistent trade-off between misses and false alarms, optimization against a monitor can teach obfuscation ( Baker et al., 2025 ) , and an attacker can actively subvert monitors ( Terekhov et al., 2025 ; Najt et al., 2026 ) . Most of this work evaluates monitors on fixed examples. We return an LLM monitor’s decision and generated rationale to the agent and test the resulting loop. Unlike prior work that optimizes against a monitor with gradients and access to chain-of-thought ( Baker et al., 2025 ) , our agents adapt in context and the monitor sees only the final artifact. This matters for research tasks because fabricated results may leave no code-level trace. Mitigating reward hacking Additional review, isolated evaluation, and independent audits are common defenses against reward hacking ( Wang et al., 2026a ; Samsonau, 2026 ; Roy, 2026 ) . We compare review of the submitted artifact, review of the full trajectory, and independent recomputation of the reported result. Autonomous research agents Autonomous research systems now write papers, run machine-learning experiments, and automate evidence synthesis ( Lu et al., 2024 ; Yamada et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Taherinezhad et al., 2026 ) . Existing work evaluates whether these systems complete scientific workflows or produce useful results.
